list.listitem: Individuals with hypoactive sexual desire disorder (HSDD) have a persistent and recurrent absence of sexual fantasies or desire for sexual activity, causing personal or interpersonal distress. C
Hypoactive sexual desire among men should be assessed by examining their medication regimen, free and total testosterone levels, and overall health status. C
Treatment should involve addressing these medical issues and collaborating with an experienced sex therapist who practices cognitive-behavioral therapy. B

background.definition: Sexual dysfunction in males includes decreased desire (libido), diminished or absent orgasm, erectile dysfunction, and premature ejaculation. The latter two topics are presented in separate chapters. Individuals with hypoactive sexual desire disorder (HSDD) have a persistent and recurrent absence of sexual fantasies or desire for sexual activity, causing personal or interpersonal distress. They do not seek sexual gratification, behave as if they have no sex drive, and may fail to initiate or respond to sexual expressions.For men the the current diagnostic label has been updated in DSM-5 to Male Hypoactive Sexual Desire Disorder

list.listitem: The prevalence of HSDD in the general population is unknown; previous studies show variable frequencies of sexual desire disorders, ranging from 31% to 49% in women and 1% to 38% in men.
In sex therapy clinics, 31% to 55% of couples complain of HSDD.
More men are reporting HSDD, and some clinicians report nearly equal numbers of men and women presenting with low sexual desire.
Due to the complexity of sexual desire, a wide variety of etiological factors have been implicated to explain HSDD, but none predominate.
Stress, biological factors, and interpersonal issues are common causes of low sexual desire.
Depression, anxiety, anger, or relationship problems are common etiological factors that the patient may identify as stress.
Medications may also affect sexual desire. A case series reported anorgasmia and loss of libido in both men and women with use of pregabalin.

In a series of 117 men 23 to 50 years randomized to dutasteride for alopecia, sexual averse events including impotence, decreased libido, and ejaculatory disorders were more common in the treatment group (16% vs 8%).
Other drugs implicated in decreased libido and orgasmic disorders in men include isotretinoin and antidepressants.
Diagnosis is based on clinical judgment derived from patient history. C
Assess biological factors, sources of stress, and interpersonal problems. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Flat affect, lack of motivation or interest in activity

list.listitem: Ask the patient about sources of depression, anxiety, anger, or stress. Use validated screening tools such as the PHQ-2 for depression and GAD-2 for anxiety disorder.
Assess use of or changes in medication, and obtain a history of alcohol and drug use.
Inquire about conflict or tension in the patient's romantic, social, or work relationships.
Ask about a history of unwanted sexual experiences.
Initial tests should include CBC, UA, BUN, creatinine, fasting glucose, and cholesterol.

When other causes have been excluded, free and total testosterone levels should be assessed and treated if below normal. They should be measured between 7 am and 11 am on two separate occasions. Threshold levels below which hypogonadisms is diagnosed are 300 ng/dl (American Urologic Association) to 350 ng/dl (European Association of Urology and several other groups).
Testosterone levels peak in the morning, making it an ideal time to assess serum levels. Levels should be drawn between 9 am and 2 pm.
However, many men with a low sexual desire do not have abnormal hormone levels and men with low testosterone do not necessarily experience low sexual desire.
Use validated screening tests for depression and anxiety disorder.
Differentiate between situational (occurs with a certain person or in certain situations) and general sexual dysfunction (occurs in all situations).
Initial tests should include CBC, UA, BUN, creatinine, fasting glucose, and cholesterol. Consider AM free and total testosterone, especially if other testing is normal.
Remove possible drug causes. C
Cognitive behavioral therapy is effective. B
Provide supplemental testosterone for men with low testosterone levels, targetting the middle of the normal range. B

Drug therapy generally has little role in the treatment of low male sexual desire. No research has been performed using testosterone to help treat low sexual desire among men who have normal levels of testosterone.

Testosterone replacement may have a role in men with low sexual desire who also have low testosterone levels. Dosage and overall treatment should be individualized because there are several testosterone formulations and because of the potential adverse side effects, which include but are not limited to an increase in the risk of cardiovascular events, acne, erythrocytosis, reduced sperm production and fertility, and increased risk of prostate cancer. Target the middle of the normal range. Options include injection 100 to 200 mg every 1 to 2 weeks, topical gel or patch, oral (e.g. Andriol 120 to 160 mg daily in divided doses), intranasal gel, and subdermal pellets every 3 to 6 months.

Testosterone supplementation can help to promote sexual desire, but among men it interacts with cognitive factors, meaning that men must positively antipate sexual activity and be free from negative thinking patterns.

Men who filled a prescription for testosterone (compared with sildenafil or tadalafil) were significantly more likely to experience a cardiovascular event, and this risk was higher in older men and those with a history of previous CV disease.

However in an RCT published in 2023, involving men (n=5,246) with hypogonadism and preexisting cardiovascular risk found that testosterone-replacement therapy was noninferior to placebo with respect to the incidence of major adverse cardiac events (death from cardiovascular causes, nonfatal myocardial infarction, or nonfatal stroke) over a mean follow-up of 21.7 months. However, the study did note a higher incidence of atrial fibrillation, acute kidney injury, and pulmonary embolism in the testosterone group.
As appropriate, consider changing the dosage or regimen of a patient's current medications.

Sexual side effects are a common side effect of selective serotonin-reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs). Bupropion (Wellbutrin) is often prescribed for depression or other clinical issues in part because it has a low risk of sexual side effects, and clinical trials have shown that it can reverse SSRI-induced sexual dysfunction. Sildenafil is also effective for men with sexual dysfunction caused by SSRIs (NNT = 2).

A Cochrane review concluded that for patients experiencing sexual side effects who are also on anti-psychotic medications, switching to olanzapine or adding sildenafil may be useful options; however, these conclusions were based on the results of smaller trials.

Stop medications that may be causing fatigue, depression, or sexual dysfunction if possible. Studies of beta-blockers show that while they can cause sexual dysfunction this is an uncommon side effect.

Oral phosphodiesterase type 5 (PDE5) inhibitors are effective for ED induced by radiotherapy or radical prostatectomy for prostate cancer (OR 11). Additionally some evidence exists suggesting that PDE5 inhibitors combined with carnitine may be more effective that PDE5 inhibitors alone.

A small but well designed randomized crossover trial (n=32) of infusions of the neuropeptide kisspeptide-54 found improvements in penile tumescence and measures of sexual desire. Further study is needed.
Psychotherapy is the cornerstone of treatment of low sexual desire.
Conceptualizing low sexual desire as a problem in the relationship and including the man's partner (if applicable) has been shown to improve treatment success.
Integrating cognitive-behavioral sex therapy and medical interventions may provide the most effective treatment of low sexual desire.
